item.title: Death by Design: Producing Racial Health Inequality in the Shadow of the Capitol — Thu Oct 8, 12:00 PM — SSRI-Gross Hall 270
item.description:
"Washington, DC, the capital of the United States, has the nation's largest racial life expectancy gap, and it has experienced many of the nation's worst epidemics, including maternal and infant mortality, homicide, heroin overdoses, and HIV/AIDS. These epidemics have disproportionately affected African Americans. Why and how does racial health inequality exist and persist? Starting from the city's founding in the late 1700s until 2022, and drawing on a range of sources-including archival material, life history interviews, and census, vital statistics, and disease surveillance data-the talk will illustrate how the physical, social, and policy design of the city contributes to the production and reproduction of disproportionate Black death."
Source: Duke University

item.title: DQC Seminar Series: Neutral-Atom Quantum Processors: From Scalable Quantum Computing to Quantum Networks — Thu Oct 8, 12:00 PM — None
item.description: Abstract: Neutral-atom arrays have emerged as a promising platform for scalable quantum information processing, combining long-lived qubits, programmable Rydberg interactions, and natural interconnection with photonic qubits. In this talk, I will discuss our efforts to develop new architectures that address key challenges in scaling neutral-atom processors toward fault-tolerant quantum computation and distributed quantum networks. I will first describe a dual-isotope rubidium architecture that provides isotope-selective control while retaining nearly identical Rydberg-Rydberg resonances, thereby enabling new approaches to mid-circuit measurement, qubit addressing, and high-fidelity entangling gates. I will then discuss our development of photonically integrated neutral-atom processors based on ytterbium atoms coupled to fiber Fabry-Perot cavities. item.title: CDVS Workshop: An Introduction to Reproducible Research Practices — Thu Oct 8, 1:00 PM — Online
item.description:
The importance of reproducibility, replication, and transparency in the research endeavor is increasingly discussed in academia. This workshop will introduce the concept of "reproducibility" and foundational strategies that can increase the reproducibility of your work particularly related to organization, documentation, literate coding techniques, version control, and archiving data and code for future access and use. We will also present a protocol, the TIER protocol, as a tool that graduate students or others can use that are first approaching reproducibility. In the second half of the workshop we will present some tools for reproducible workflows like git and its integrations with RStudio and Zenodo, and provide resources for hands-on learning and practice.This event is open to non-Duke participants. This workshop is eligible for 2 hours of Graduate School RCR Credit (GS714) and 200-level faculty and staff RCR.
Source: Duke University

item.title: Distinguished Seminar Series with Dr. James Duncan — Thu Oct 8, 3:00 PM — Wilkinson 021
item.description:
Neuroimage Analysis in Autism: from Model-Based Estimation to Data-driven Learning
Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has been shown to be helpful for the study of autism spectrum disorders (ASD). This talk will describe the evolution of efforts in this area within our group that carry promise for producing objective biomarkers for ASD, as well as predicting patient response to a behavioral therapy known as Pivotal Response Treatment (PRT), using task-based fMRI. Such biomarkers would provide an important step for better understanding the underlying pathophysiology of ASD that could help with objective and personalized diagnosis, provide new targets for development of new treatments, and provide a way to monitor patient progress. Initially a robust, group-wise unified Bayesian framework to detect both hyper and hypo-active communities from connectivity maps will be described. item.description:
The US Department of Energy's Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) is a huge and diverse research center located in eastern Tennessee near Knoxville. Its mission is incredibly diverse: biology and the environment, clean energy including fission and fusion, isotope production, basic physical sciences, national security in multiple contexts, neutron sciences, and supercomputing.⁠ ⁠ You are invited to a presentation given by William Jenks of ORNL's Office of Research Education to learn about ORNL's many opportunities for summer internships and other student programs aimed at undergraduates and recent graduates. The session will give you an idea of different research areas and give you the keys to a successful application. Applications for Summer 2026 will be announced on the ORNL Website.⁠ ⁠ The presentation will give information on how to apply for and successfully obtain a Summer 2027 internship at ORNL.⁠

item.title: Duke University Wind Symphony: Overtures in October — Thu Oct 8, 7:30 PM — Baldwin Auditorium
item.description:
The Duke Wind Symphony celebrates the season with Overtures in October, a program showcasing the brilliance and versatility of the concert overture. From the youthful energy of Mendelssohn's Overture for Winds in C Major to contemporary works by Óscar Navarro and Joseph Willcox Jenkins, the program highlights the overture's enduring ability to captivate audiences and tell compelling musical stories. These works are complemented by evocative reflections on the season from Julie Giroux and Eric Whitacre. Whitacre's October captures the warmth and nostalgia of autumn, while Giroux's Riften Wed offers a poignant meditation on love, commitment, and resilience in the face of uncertainty.
A highlight of the concert is the world premiere of a new work by Flavio Lamelle, adding a fresh chapter to the wind band repertoire.
Filled with lyricism, excitement, and imagination, Overtures in October brings the sounds and spirit of autumn to Baldwin Auditorium.
This event is free and open to the pub

item.title: Workshop: Jewish Literatures Beyond Zionism — Fri Oct 9 — None
item.description:
"Jewish Literatures Beyond Zionism" workshop is being held at SUNY-Binghamton.
This workshop explores contemporary approaches to the study of modern Jewish literature, with particular attention to questions of identity, nationalism, diaspora, memory, and transnational literary exchange. Participants will examine how recent historical and political developments have prompted scholars to reconsider established frameworks in Jewish literary studies and to explore alternative interpretive models.
Bringing together researchers from a range of disciplinary perspectives, the workshop will address topics such as diasporic Jewish literatures, comparative minority literatures, translation and cultural circulation, Sephardic and Mizrahi writing, gender and sexuality, decolonial methodologies, and the relationship between literature and social movements. The workshop aims to foster rigorous scholarly dialogue on the diverse histories, languages, and futures of Jewish literary cultures.

item.title: NC Public Librarian Certification Commission — Fri Oct 30, 10:30 AM — DNCR
item.description:
The NC Public Librarian Certification Commission was formed in 1936 to set minimum standards for public librarians to protect and maintain public library resources, to assure professional management and administration of library services, to meet the personnel requirements for State Aid administered by the Library of NC, and to guarantee the best possible public library service to all North Carolinians.
The North Carolina General Statute 143B-68 states that the commission must be comprised of: the Chairman of the public libraries section of NCLA, two individuals named by the Governor upon nomination of the NCLA, the dean of a State or regionally accredited graduate school of librarianship in North Carolina appointed by the Governor, and one member at large appointed by the Governor. Commission members appointed by the Governor serve 4-year terms, all others serve 2-year terms.
